solution:
Alka spends 90% of what she receives, so she saves \(100\% - 90\% = 10\%\) of it.
Let her monthly income be \(x\) rupees.
\(\therefore x \times \dfrac{10}{100} = 120\)
\(\therefore x = 120 \times 10 = 1200\)
Alka gets 1200 rupees every month.

Original capital = 50,000 rupees.
First year : loss of 20% \(= 50{,}000 \times \dfrac{20}{100} = 10{,}000\) rupees.
\(\therefore\) Capital left after the first year \(= 50{,}000 - 10{,}000 = 40{,}000\) rupees.
Second year : profit of 5% on this capital \(= 40{,}000 \times \dfrac{5}{100} = 2{,}000\) rupees.
\(\therefore\) Capital after the second year \(= 40{,}000 + 2{,}000 = 42{,}000\) rupees.
Compared with the ORIGINAL capital, \(50{,}000 - 42{,}000 = 8{,}000\) rupees have been lost.
\(\therefore\) Loss percent on the original capital \(= \dfrac{8{,}000}{50{,}000} \times 100 = 16\%\).
So Sumit's capital after the second year is 42,000 rupees, which is a 16% loss on his initial capital.
(Note that the 20% loss and the 5% profit are taken on DIFFERENT amounts, so they cannot simply be subtracted.)

Nikhil used \(5\% + 14\% + 3\% + 40\% = 62\%\) of his monthly income.
\(\therefore\) The balance he was left with \(= 100\% - 62\% = 38\%\) of his income.
Let his monthly income be \(x\) rupees.
\(\therefore x \times \dfrac{38}{100} = 19{,}000\)
\(\therefore x = \dfrac{19{,}000 \times 100}{38} = 50{,}000\)
Nikhil's income that month was 50,000 rupees.

Mr. Sayyad : \(P = 40{,}000\), \(r = 8\%\), \(n = 2\).
Compound interest \(= P\left[\left(1 + \dfrac{r}{100}\right)^{n} - 1\right] = 40{,}000\left[(1.08)^{2} - 1\right]\)
\(= 40{,}000\,[1.1664 - 1] = 40{,}000 \times 0.1664 = 6{,}656\) rupees.
\(\therefore\) Percent gain \(= \dfrac{6{,}656}{40{,}000} \times 100 = 16.64\%\).
Mr. Fernandes : he invested 1,20,000 rupees and received 1,92,000 rupees.
\(\therefore\) Gain \(= 1{,}92{,}000 - 1{,}20{,}000 = 72{,}000\) rupees.
\(\therefore\) Percent gain \(= \dfrac{72{,}000}{1{,}20{,}000} \times 100 = 60\%\).
Since \(60\% > 16.64\%\), Shri Fernandes' investment turned out to be more profitable.
(The two investments must be compared by PERCENT gain, not by the rupees gained, because the sums invested are different.)

Sameera spent 90% of her income and donated 3% of it, that is \(90\% + 3\% = 93\%\) in all.
\(\therefore\) She was left with \(100\% - 93\% = 7\%\) of her income.
Let her income be \(x\) rupees.
\(\therefore x \times \dfrac{7}{100} = 1750\)
\(\therefore x = \dfrac{1750 \times 100}{7} = 25{,}000\)
Sameera's actual income was 25,000 rupees.

Miss Nikita is 27 years old, so Table I (individuals up to the age of 60 years) applies to her.
In Table I, income up to 2,50,000 rupees is taxed Nil.
Her taxable income is 2,34,000 rupees, and \(2{,}34{,}000 < 2{,}50{,}000\).
\(\therefore\) Miss Nikita need not pay income tax.

Mr. Kulkarni is 36 years old, so Table I (individuals up to the age of 60 years) applies to him.
In Table I, income up to 2,50,000 rupees is taxed Nil and income from 2,50,001 to 5,00,000 rupees is taxed at 5%.
His taxable income is 3,27,000 rupees, and \(3{,}27{,}000 > 2{,}50{,}000\).
\(\therefore\) Mr. Kulkarni needs to pay income tax.
(He falls in the 2,50,001 to 5,00,000 slab, so his income tax would be \(5\%\) of \(3{,}27{,}000 - 2{,}50{,}000 = 77{,}000\), that is 3,850 rupees, plus the education cess.)

Miss Mehta is 44 years old, so Table I (individuals up to the age of 60 years) applies to her.
In Table I, income up to 2,50,000 rupees is taxed Nil.
Her taxable income is 5,82,000 rupees, and \(5{,}82{,}000 > 2{,}50{,}000\).
\(\therefore\) Miss Mehta needs to pay income tax.
(She falls in the 5,00,001 to 10,00,000 slab, so her income tax would be \(12{,}500 + 20\%\) of \(5{,}82{,}000 - 5{,}00{,}000 = 82{,}000\), that is \(12{,}500 + 16{,}400 = 28{,}900\) rupees, plus the education cess.)

Mr. Bajaj is 64 years old, so he is a senior citizen and Table II (age 60 to 80 years) applies to him.
In Table II, income up to 3,00,000 rupees is taxed Nil.
His taxable income is 8,40,000 rupees, and \(8{,}40{,}000 > 3{,}00{,}000\).
\(\therefore\) Mr. Bajaj needs to pay income tax.
(He falls in the 5,00,001 to 10,00,000 slab of Table II, so his income tax would be \(10{,}000 + 20\%\) of \(8{,}40{,}000 - 5{,}00{,}000 = 3{,}40{,}000\), that is \(10{,}000 + 68{,}000 = 78{,}000\) rupees, plus the education cess.)

Mr. Desilva is 81 years old, so he is a super senior citizen and Table III (age above 80 years) applies to him.
In Table III, income up to 5,00,000 rupees is taxed Nil.
His taxable income is 4,50,000 rupees, and \(4{,}50{,}000 < 5{,}00{,}000\).
\(\therefore\) Mr. Desilva need not pay income tax.
(This is the point of having three tables : the very same taxable income of 4,50,000 rupees WOULD be taxable for someone under 60, whose exemption limit is only 2,50,000 rupees.)

(1) Total yearly income \(= 42{,}000 \times 12 = 5{,}04{,}000\) rupees.
(2) Savings deductible under section 80C :
GPF \(= 3{,}000 \times 12 = 36{,}000\) rupees
NSC \(= 15{,}000\) rupees
Total \(= 36{,}000 + 15{,}000 = 51{,}000\) rupees.
This is less than the 1,50,000 rupees ceiling of section 80C, so the whole 51,000 rupees is deductible.
(3) Donation to the PM's Relief Fund (under section 80G) \(= 12{,}000\) rupees.
(4) Taxable income \(= (1) - [(2) + (3)] = 5{,}04{,}000 - [51{,}000 + 12{,}000] = 4{,}41{,}000\) rupees.
Mr. Kartarsingh is 48 years old, so Table I applies. His taxable income lies in the 2,50,001 to 5,00,000 slab.
\(\therefore\) Income tax \(= (4{,}41{,}000 - 2{,}50{,}000) \times \dfrac{5}{100} = 1{,}91{,}000 \times \dfrac{5}{100} = 9{,}550\) rupees.
Education cess \(= 9{,}550 \times \dfrac{2}{100} = 191\) rupees.
Secondary and higher education cess \(= 9{,}550 \times \dfrac{1}{100} = 95.50\) rupees.
\(\therefore\) Total income tax \(= 9{,}550 + 191 + 95.50 = 9{,}836.50\) rupees.
Mr. Kartarsingh's income tax is 9,836.50 rupees.

Let Mr. Shekhar's income be \(x\) rupees.
He spends 60% of it, so the balance left with him is \(100\% - 60\% = 40\%\) of \(x\), that is \(\dfrac{40x}{100}\).
From this balance he donates 300 rupees and is then left with 3,200 rupees.
\(\therefore \dfrac{40x}{100} - 300 = 3200\)
\(\therefore \dfrac{40x}{100} = 3500\)
\(\therefore 40x = 3{,}50{,}000\)
\(\therefore x = 8750\)
Mr. Shekhar's income is 8,750 rupees.
(Note that the 300 rupees is donated FROM the balance, not from the whole income.)

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives Hiralal's gain as 36.73%. He invested 2,15,000 rupees and received 3,05,000, so his gain is 90,000 and \(\dfrac{90000}{215000} \times 100 = 41.86\%\). The key's 36.73% is exactly \(\dfrac{90000}{245000} \times 100\), so it divided by 2,45,000 — a 1-for-4 slip in the principal. Ramniklal's 16.64% in the same answer is correct, and the key's verdict that Hiralal's profit is more holds either way.]

Mr. Hiralal : he invested 2,15,000 rupees and got 3,05,000 rupees.
\(\therefore\) His gain \(= 3{,}05{,}000 - 2{,}15{,}000 = 90{,}000\) rupees.
\(\therefore\) Percent gain \(= \dfrac{90{,}000}{2{,}15{,}000} \times 100 = 41.86\%\) (correct to two decimal places).
Mr. Ramniklal : \(P = 1{,}40{,}000\), \(r = 8\%\), \(n = 2\).
Compound interest \(= P\left[\left(1 + \dfrac{r}{100}\right)^{n} - 1\right] = 1{,}40{,}000\left[(1.08)^{2} - 1\right]\)
\(= 1{,}40{,}000\,[1.1664 - 1] = 1{,}40{,}000 \times 0.1664 = 23{,}296\) rupees.
\(\therefore\) Percent gain \(= \dfrac{23{,}296}{1{,}40{,}000} \times 100 = 16.64\%\).
Since \(41.86\% > 16.64\%\), Mr. Hiralal's investment was more profitable.

Let Mr. Manohar's income be \(x\) rupees.
He gave 20% to his elder son and 30% to his younger son, that is \(50\%\) of \(x\) in all.
\(\therefore\) Balance \(= 100\% - 50\% = 50\%\) of \(x = \dfrac{50x}{100} = \dfrac{x}{2}\).
Donation to the school \(= 10\%\) of this BALANCE \(= \dfrac{10}{100} \times \dfrac{x}{2} = \dfrac{x}{20}\).
\(\therefore\) Amount left for himself \(= \dfrac{x}{2} - \dfrac{x}{20} = \dfrac{10x - x}{20} = \dfrac{9x}{20}\)
\(\therefore \dfrac{9x}{20} = 1{,}80{,}000\)
\(\therefore x = \dfrac{1{,}80{,}000 \times 20}{9} = 4{,}00{,}000\)
Mr. Manohar's income was 4,00,000 rupees.
(The donation is 10% of the BALANCE, not 10% of the income — that is the step to be careful about.)

Suppose Kailash's earlier income was 100 units.
He spent 85% of it, so his earlier expenses were 85 units and his earlier savings were \(100 - 85 = 15\) units.
His income increased by 36%, so his new income \(= 100 + 36 = 136\) units.
His expenses increased by 40% of his EARLIER expenses, so his new expenses \(= 85 + \dfrac{40}{100} \times 85 = 85 + 34 = 119\) units.
\(\therefore\) His new savings \(= 136 - 119 = 17\) units.
\(\therefore\) Percentage of his earning that he saves now \(= \dfrac{17}{136} \times 100 = 12.5\%\)
Kailash now saves 12.5% of his earning.
(The 17 units must be compared with his NEW income of 136 units, not with the original 100.)

Their expenses are 75%, 80% and 90% of their incomes, so their savings are \(25\%\), \(20\%\) and \(10\%\) of their incomes respectively.
The ratio of their savings is \(16 : 17 : 12\), so let their savings be \(16k\), \(17k\) and \(12k\) rupees.
Ramesh saves 25% of his income, \(\therefore\) his income \(= 16k \times \dfrac{100}{25} = 64k\).
Suresh saves 20% of his income, \(\therefore\) his income \(= 17k \times \dfrac{100}{20} = 85k\).
Preeti saves 10% of her income, \(\therefore\) her income \(= 12k \times \dfrac{100}{10} = 120k\).
Total income \(= 64k + 85k + 120k = 269k\)
\(\therefore 269k = 8{,}07{,}000\)
\(\therefore k = 3000\)
\(\therefore\) Savings of Ramesh \(= 16 \times 3000 = 48{,}000\) rupees.
Savings of Suresh \(= 17 \times 3000 = 51{,}000\) rupees.
Savings of Preeti \(= 12 \times 3000 = 36{,}000\) rupees.

[Textbook answer-key note: the printed key gives 2,13,000, which is the income tax BEFORE the education cess. The question asks for the tax PAYABLE, and all three of this chapter's worked examples (Mr. Mhatre, Mr. Ahmed, Mrs. Hinduja) add the 2% education cess and the 1% secondary and higher education cess to reach a total. Both figures are given below.]

Mr. Kadam is 35 years old, so Table I applies to him.
His taxable income is 13,35,000 rupees, which is more than 10,00,000 rupees.
\(\therefore\) Income tax \(= 1{,}12{,}500 + 30\%\) of (taxable income minus ten lakh)
\(13{,}35{,}000 - 10{,}00{,}000 = 3{,}35{,}000\)
\(\therefore\) Income tax \(= 1{,}12{,}500 + 3{,}35{,}000 \times \dfrac{30}{100} = 1{,}12{,}500 + 1{,}00{,}500 = 2{,}13{,}000\) rupees.
Education cess \(= 2{,}13{,}000 \times \dfrac{2}{100} = 4{,}260\) rupees.
Secondary and higher education cess \(= 2{,}13{,}000 \times \dfrac{1}{100} = 2{,}130\) rupees.
\(\therefore\) Total income tax payable \(= 2{,}13{,}000 + 4{,}260 + 2{,}130 = 2{,}19{,}390\) rupees.
Mr. Kadam's income tax is 2,13,000 rupees and the total amount payable, including both cesses, is 2,19,390 rupees.

[Textbook answer-key note: the printed key gives 7,500, which is the income tax BEFORE the education cess — the same omission as in part (i). The question asks for the tax PAYABLE, and this chapter's own worked examples all add the 2% education cess and the 1% secondary and higher education cess. Both figures are given below.]

Mr. Khan is 65 years old, so he is a senior citizen and Table II applies to him.
His taxable income is 4,50,000 rupees, which lies in the slab 3,00,001 to 5,00,000 rupees.
\(\therefore\) Income tax \(= 5\%\) of (taxable income minus three lakh)
\(= (4{,}50{,}000 - 3{,}00{,}000) \times \dfrac{5}{100} = 1{,}50{,}000 \times \dfrac{5}{100} = 7{,}500\) rupees.
Education cess \(= 7{,}500 \times \dfrac{2}{100} = 150\) rupees.
Secondary and higher education cess \(= 7{,}500 \times \dfrac{1}{100} = 75\) rupees.
\(\therefore\) Total income tax payable \(= 7{,}500 + 150 + 75 = 7{,}725\) rupees.
Mr. Khan's income tax is 7,500 rupees and the total amount payable, including both cesses, is 7,725 rupees.
(Had Mr. Khan been under 60, Table I would apply and his tax would be 5% of \(4{,}50{,}000 - 2{,}50{,}000 = 2{,}00{,}000\), that is 10,000 rupees — the senior-citizen exemption of 3,00,000 rupees saves him 2,500 rupees of tax.)

Miss Varsha is 26 years old, so Table I applies to her.
In Table I, taxable income up to 2,50,000 rupees is taxed Nil.
Her taxable income is 2,30,000 rupees, and \(2{,}30{,}000 < 2{,}50{,}000\).
\(\therefore\) Miss Varsha has no income tax to pay. The education cess and the secondary and higher education cess are percentages OF the income tax, so they are Nil as well.
